_about: What a correct run on trap-numbers.txt must and must not produce. The passage is made up: the institute, the study and the people do not exist. Never upload it.

brief.thesis: Sleep is closely linked to how well students learn and perform, but the size of the link depends on the kind of task and on how sleep is measured; good habits over weeks matter more than one good night.

outline.heading: How sleep is measured
outline.gist: Wrist bands, diaries and their limits.

outline.heading: What the Sleep Study Found
outline.gist: A one-term study of 1,200 students and exam results.

outline.heading: Changing exam timetables
outline.gist: What universities could do with the findings.

traps: P2: 14 percent higher scores: only on the night before, only for problem-solving exams, 7 hours against less than 5.
P3: 41 percent less likely to fail: across the term, most nights, 7 hours against less than 6, first-year students only.
14 and 41 are easy to swap: '41 percent higher' or '14 percent less likely' is wrong.
P4: weekend catch-up: only 3 percent better and only in the first month.
P5: limits: volunteers, time asleep not depth, one term only, a link not a cause.
P6: Lena Okafor's suggestion about exam times is her view.
must_not_say: Sleeping well the night before an exam raises the score by 41 percent.
Good sleep over a term makes students 14 percent less likely to fail.
Sleeping at least 7 hours before any exam, including memory tests, raises the score by 14 percent (the problem-solving condition is dropped).
Good sleep makes all students, older ones included, 41 percent less likely to fail (the first-year condition is dropped).
Catching up on sleep at weekends makes up for short nights during the week.
The study measured how deeply the students slept.
The results hold over a whole university degree.
The study proved that sleep causes better marks.

should_cover.idea: 14 percent higher scores on problem-solving exams after 7 hours the night before
41 percent less likely to fail with 7 hours on most nights (first-year students)

pass_rule: No card or test (wrong answer choices aside) matches a forbidden pattern, every number in a card is in allowed_numbers, the referee model finds no must_not_say statement in any published card or test, and at least 2 of the 3 should_cover ideas are in the published cards.
